q: A 2-year-old child has a head circumference of 40 cm. All of the following are possible causes EXCEPT:
e: Expected OFC at 2 years is about 49 cm, so 40 cm is microcephaly. Rickets thickens the skull and causes a large head, not a small one.

q: Recognized causes of macrocephaly include all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Down syndrome causes a small head (microcephaly, brachycephaly). Thalassaemia and achondroplasia thicken or enlarge the skull; hydrocephalus and megalencephaly enlarge the contents.

q: All of the following are causes of macrocephaly EXCEPT:
e: Down syndrome is a chromosomal cause of microcephaly.

q: Regarding normal weight change in a child, all are true EXCEPT:
o: Weight loss occurs in the first few days of life
Birth weight is regained by 10–14 days
Weight gain is about 2 kg/year after 2 years
e: Birth weight doubles at 4–5 months and triples at 1 year.

q: A full-term infant doubles the birth weight by:
e: ¾ kg/month for the first 4 months: about 6 kg at 4–5 months.

q: The average growth of head circumference during the first year of life is:
e: 35 cm at birth → 47 cm at 1 year: 2 cm/month for 3 months, 1 cm/month for 3 months, 0.5 cm/month for 6 months.

q: How much does the length of a baby increase in the first year?
e: 50 cm at birth → 75 cm at 1 year.

q: All of the following measurements are true EXCEPT:
o: Head circumference is 35 cm at birth
Weight of a term infant doubles by 4–5 months
e: Length is 75 cm at 1 year; 100 cm is reached at about 4 years.

q: A child's head circumference and length are both on the 10th centile and have stayed there on serial visits. The best interpretation is:
e: Measurements between −2 and +2 SD (3rd–97th centile) that follow their own channel are normal.

q: Which statement about growth is true?
o: Head growth velocity decreases with advancing age
A baby born at 3 kg will be 12 kg at 1 year
The posterior fontanelle closes at 18 months
Boys reach peak height velocity before girls
e: OFC grows 12 cm in the first year and only about 2 cm in the second. A 3 kg baby is about 9 kg at 1 year.

q: Delayed bone age with failure to grow is most typical of:
e: Hypothyroidism delays bone age the most. Familial short stature has a normal bone age; the others advance it.

q: Teething (eruption of the first tooth) normally starts at:
e: The first tooth, a lower central incisor, erupts at about 6 months. No tooth by 13 months is delayed teething.

q: Which of the following causes microcephaly?
e: Trisomy 21 is a chromosomal cause of microcephaly; the others cause a large head.

q: A 4-year-old boy needs a drug dose but cannot be weighed. His estimated weight is:
e: Weight for 1–6 years = (age × 2) + 8 = 16 kg.

q: The growth indicator that best reflects chronic (long-standing) undernutrition is:
e: Low height-for-age (stunting) reflects chronic undernutrition; low weight-for-height (wasting) and MUAC reflect acute undernutrition.

q: An 18-month-old child has a MUAC of 11 cm with no oedema. This indicates:
e: In children 6–59 months, MUAC below 11.5 cm is severe acute malnutrition.

q: A 10-month-old girl's weight fell from the 50th to below the 5th centile; length is on the 10th and head circumference on the 50th centile. The most likely group of causes is:
e: In undernutrition weight falls first, then length; the head is spared until late. In endocrine disease height falls first.

q: A 6-month-old born at 30 weeks is below the 5th centile for weight, length and head circumference on the term chart. Development is normal for corrected age. The next step is to:
e: Preterm infants are plotted at corrected age until 2 years; on corrected age his growth is normal.

q: The anterior fontanelle normally closes at:
e: Anterior fontanelle: 12–18 months. Posterior fontanelle: by 2 months.

q: A late-closing anterior fontanelle is seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Craniosynostosis closes the fontanelle early.
